item.title: Please don’t stretch your app for foldables
item.description: What happens when the screen isn’t a fixed constraint?Foldables have existed in the market since 2019 with the Samsung Galaxy Fold, but it’s really only been an “Android thing.” And if your app primarily serves the U.S. market (where most smartphones are iOS), foldables haven’t been a priority to design for. Even with an Android customer base, only a small percentage of those devices are foldables.But this foldable conversation is different now with Apple’s iPhone Duo announcement. This one foldable has caused more buzz than the entire Android foldable ecosystem ever has.Adaptive app examples from Airbnb and Spotify across form factorsIf you’ve never considered designing for foldables for your native app experience, it’s understandable (and common). It’s hard to get design/engineering buy-in when so few people will use the app on such a unique form factor.Now there’s a greater argument. iPhone Duo has a strong sales forecast and is projected to take 25% of the foldable market by end of 2026; only to increase from there.So if you’re starting from square-one and have no idea how to address foldables, it’s good to have a foundation to both understand the form factor and the expectations between iOS and Android. Let’s get into some best practices to integrate iOS and Android foldables into your design process.Core principlesFoldables seem complex because they combine multiple screen sizes, aspect ratios, orientations, and postures in a single device. To maintain a good experience with foldables, you need to adapt hierarchy, layout, and controls to the available space and how the device is being used (don’t worry, we’ll get there).Design for available space vs. the deviceInstead of asking “What does this screen look like on a Galaxy Z Fold/iPhone Duo?”, ask “What does this experience need to do when the available window becomes wider, narrower, taller, or split?”The same designs should be able to accommodate:Standard phonesFlip and book-style foldablesTablets or multitasking windowsSupporting different layout sizes, via Android Developer documentationPreserve hierarchyWhen available space changes, the UI doesn’t need to remain visually identical.What should adapt:Navigation & control placementContent density / amount of content displayedNumber of columnsSupporting information / image sizeWhat should not adapt:Primary task & key actionsContent hierarchyNavigation model & user’s current contextFor example:When the iPhone Duo is closed, content is presented in a drill-down style with List → Tap → Detail. Versus when opened, the same content is presented simultaneously with the list on the left and details on the right of the device.Don’t stretch the UIYou may think allowing the UI layout to expand across a large device display is an easy solution to fill in the space, but Android specifically asks for the usage of panes and adaptive layouts.Best practices:Add maximum content widths & larger gutters between elementsUse multiple columns & supporting panesEnsure grids are responsiveAvoid:Extremely long text lines (line length should be about 50 characters)Oversized cards, modals, bottom sheets, and imageryFull-width buttons spanning a tablet-sized displayExcessive empty spaceUnited’s notification settings span the entire screen when a Google Pixel Pro Fold is openDesign around the hingeDepending on the device, the hinge (where the device folds) can impact touch interactions, content readability, and available layout space.Avoid positioning important content across the hinge, like:Buttons or form fields (especially critical navigation controls)Dialogs or menusImportant text or imagerySince the hinge’s crease is quite visible in some foldables, it’s best to look at the hinge as the device’s “natural divider.” Both Android and iOS recommend making layouts “hinge-aware,” and to adapt layouts around it.Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 4’s visible crease; via The VergeThink in “panes”A useful mental model when designing for foldables is:Traditional phone → 1 primary paneOpened foldable/tablet → 2+ related panesCommon layout patterns using panes include:List → detail: Use for search results, messages/emails, or settingsNavigation → content: Use when persistent navigation becomes valuable on a larger displayPrimary content → supporting content/controls: Useful for media, maps, or formsUnderstand foldable statesA foldable can have different experiences depending on how it is positioned (called “poses” on iOS and “postures” on Android).Closed (folded)The device behaves more like a traditional phone, and uses the outer display of the foldable.Prioritize what you typically would for native-mobile experiences, like:Essential information & primary/quick actionsCompact navigationOne-handed interactionsExample display layout:Email inbox list → Tap → Individual email detailsOpen (flat)The device provides more space compared to the closed state, and uses the inner displays (they open like a book or clam-shell).Use the additional space to:Reduce navigation steps & increase content visibilityProvide persistent navigation & show additional controlsReveal supporting information by introducing a second paneExample display layout (for book-style):Email inbox list (left pane) | Individual email details (right pane)How Slack displays on iPhone Duo in open state; via AppleHalf-open (tabletop)The device is partially folded along the hinge in portrait orientation, which creates an upper and lower region.Upper region: Used for content, video, or informationLower region: Used for controls or additional interactions that correspond to the upper regionExample display layout:Upper region includes a video, and lower region includes the playback controls (how Netflix may appear)Note: This state may not be needed for all experiences; it’s more of an enhancement if the product could benefit from supporting it (i.e., watching videos or playing games).Android foldable in tabletop state for playing video game; via Digital TrendsHalf-open (book)The device is partially folded along the hinge in landscape orientation, and creates two distinct regions in the left and right screens (like a split view).This state works well for:Reading or reference content for related pieces of infoList → detail viewsNavigation → content viewsExample display layouts are similar to the “open” state, but content is divided by the device hinge. This can be used to run 2 apps simultaneously.Adapt to changing configurationsA user can be in the middle of a task and decide to change their foldable’s orientation (landscape → portrait) or posture (folded → unfolded). When this happens, the app’s navigation, controls, sheets, and other interactive elements need to adapt while preserving the user’s context and maintaining platform conventions.The same task should remain available across configurations, but you need to define how the presentation responds to best use the available space.NavigationCompact view:Use mobile navigation patterns (bottom nav, nav stacks, and back navigation)Keep frequently used navigation within reachExpanded view:Use persistent navigation, navigation rails, or side navigationDo not stretch mobile navigation patterns across a large displayWhen the device changes configuration:Preserve the user’s current location, info hierarchy, and navigation stateDon’t unexpectedly reset the navigation stackSpotify navigation and content transition from closed to open state on Google Pixel Pro FoldSheets, dialogs & overlaysCompact view:Use bottom sheets and full-screen presentations for focused tasksKeep actions within comfortable reachExpanded view:Use centered dialogs, partial-width sheet, side panel, or secondary panesDon’t stretch a mobile sheet or dialog to fill the entire displayAvoid placing important content or controls across the foldSpotify bottom sheets transition to partial-width on Google’s Pixel Pro FoldTransitionsThe transition animation from folded → unfolded should feel continuous and not increase cognitive load.Prioritize:Preserve state and contextAnimate meaningful repositioning to keep the user’s focusMaintain content hierarchyAvoid:Full-screen reloads or loss of scroll positionResetting navigation or form fieldsAbruptly changing the user’s taskPlatform specific guidanceiOSApple’s new foldable guidelines introduce several concepts you should consider in your design process. Apple’s arrangement APIs help create layouts that dynamically respond to size and aspect ratio.For these APIs to work best, you need to define layout rules, size classes, reserved regions, and how components reflow when the device state changes.I. Use “size classes”Size classes indicate how much horizontal and vertical space is available to an iOS app’s interface. For foldables, design around Compact and Regular size classes vs. creating custom designs for each pose.Compact: Horizontal=Narrow, Vertical=ShortRegular: Horizontal=Wide, Vertical=TallCompact and regular size classes represented on large display; via Apple LayoutsII. Respect “reserved regions”iPhone Duo has physical areas, called reserved regions, that can affect usable space. This is similar to safe areas (like the system UI) in Apple’s ecosystem, and includes the hinge and outer/inner display cameras.Your design needs to account for the device’s reserved regions, hinge, and safe areas to determine what area is available to your app content.Hinge and inner camera reserved regions on iPhone Duo; via AppleNote: If you’re interested in learning more about designing for iPhone Duo, Apple has released some helpful, short videos (‘Get ready for iPhone Duo’).AndroidAndroid’s adaptive design guidelines are built around the available app window vs. physical screen size. The window size can change when a device is unfolded, rotated, or used in multi-window mode, so layouts must respond to the space available to the app.I. Use “window size classes”Android’s window size classes determine how your layout should adapt as the available app window changes; similar to iOS size classes.Compact: Narrow phone-sized windowMedium: Larger phone or unfolded foldable-sized windowExpanded: Tablet-sized or large foldable windowWidth-based window size classes; via Android developer documentationII. Design for “edge-to-edge” and window-insetsAndroid uses edge-to-edge layouts, with edge-to-edge enforced for apps targeting Android 15 (API 35) and later. Use window-insets to account for system UI and other areas, like camera cutouts, that can overlap your content. Window-insets are similar to the “reserved regions” in iOS.Consider insets for:Status and navigation barsDisplay cutouts (cameras–placement differs per device manufacturer)System gestures (swiping left or right from the far edge → Android “Back” action)On-screen keyboardNote: If you don’t have access to an Android device, you can download “Android Studio” and use the ‘Virtual Device Manager” to access Google Pixel devices ranging between form factors.Foldable design checklistHere are some questions to review as you create designs for all different types of device configurations. Once designs are implemented, it’s ideal to pressure test your app in each device configuration (folded, unfolded, half-open, split screen, & portrait/landscape orientations).LayoutAre maximum content widths defined vs. stretching?Does content reflow appropriately?Are different aspect ratios and orientations supported?Fold / hingeDo important content and UI controls avoid the fold?Do dialogs and sheets avoid the fold?Are controls reachable in every configuration?NavigationDoes navigation adapt to available space?Does the user maintain their place when unfolding or folding?Is navigation still understandable when the window is resized?ContentDoes content remain understandable when moved?Are text lines constrained for readability?Do images maintain appropriate aspect ratios?Foldables aren’t just bigger screens. They introduce multiple ways for people to use the same device, and your app needs to adapt to those possibilities without making the experience feel unfamiliar or unexpected.So please don’t stretch your app to fill the space. Design for the space that’s available.Please don’t stretch your app for foldables was originally published in UX Collective on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

item.title: Rethinking writing in the world of design and AI
item.description: What 100 articles taught me about thinking, friction, and the Shoggoth on the horizonOne hundred design articles, each a small act of thinking: a growing archive of ideas, experiments, doubts, and discoveries, made in the shadow of AI. (image source: Yeo)I can’t believe it. I have finally written my 100th design article. What was thought to be an impossible task when I first picked up the pen (or the keyboard) back in 2022 proved to be wrong. Today, I can finally claim a huge sense of achievement and relief. Not because I am done with writing — far from it — but because I continue to have much to say about design.And as I write a new article every fortnightly, I come to understand myself a little better. The past me isn’t the same as the present me and most likely won’t be the same as the future me. How I think, how I feel, and how I act on those thoughts and emotions have changed too. Oscar Wilde says it best:If you cannot write well, you cannot think well. And if you cannot think well, others will do your thinking for you.”These days, the fear of not thinking well has not gone away. You might think that after writing 100 articles, I have the mettle of regurgitating new ideas into prose, that I have a magic box tucked away in my mind that could summon the most original thinking. I have none of those. Instead, I feel like one of the scared crews in Homer’s Odyssey, wondering what monster lurks on the island and when my hero’s journey ends.After 100 articles, I still feel like one of Odysseus’ crew: sailing onwards, unsure of what waits beyond the next horizon (image source: nordiskpost)In 2026, that boss-level monster on the horizon isn’t a mythical Cyclops. It’s something far more amorphous. I like to call it the Shoggoth: a sprawling entity with grotesque tentacles spilling out of its body while donning a placid, smiling mask. If this is new to you, the Shoggoth originates from the imagination of science-fiction writer H.P. Lovecraft. As writer Jürgen Gravestein puts it, they are shapeshifting creatures created as an instruction-following, slave-like workforce, always under their creators’ control. A bit like large language models. And if you squint really hard, you might actually see the logo of Claude.I admit. As a designer and a writer, I have a love-hate relationship with AI. I love it for the pseudo-intellectual discourse I have with a sycophant agent. With its seductive charm and frictionless vibing, I could easily generate an article in an evening with a few prompts, saving me time to spend it with my family or doom scrolling on social media (with my wife).And yet I hate it for how I have fallen prey to deceptive seamlessness without the same struggle of writing that my past self used to experience with the first few articles before ChatGPT. What made this ironic is that while technology is meant for good, the struggle is equally virtuous. Isn’t that what learning is about?The Shoggoth: an unknowable machine underneath, made friendly by a smiling mask (image source: Yeo)Some designers may view the struggle of writing as a waste of time, thus resorting to AI for quick fixes in their portfolio and work. I tend to agree that AI is a gamechanger for pointless emails. What I am more cautious about is whether we should outsource everything to AI. As Wildes framed it, do we want AI to do the thinking for us?Anyone who reads and writes about design would know about Fabric Teixeira’s writing. As the co-founder of UX Collective, he advocates for designers to write because not only does our portfolio become multi-dimensional beyond pixels, but it also sharpens our craft and brings communities together. His view on AI is just as valid:“The value of your actual voice, your real stories, your screw-ups, and your wins are even more valuable. The need for genuine human perspectives has never been higher.”In many ways, this echoes the exact point of Michael Bierut’s legendary 100-Day Project. Bierut taught us that discipline is the ultimate vehicle for creative inspiration and that real growth only happens when we embrace the friction of repetition. My four-year timeline may have stretched his original design sprint of 100 days, but the core lesson remains identical: by refusing to outsource the labour of thinking, I forced myself to evolve.Michael Bierut’s daily sketchbook drawings, made from photographs in The New York Times during his own sustained creative practice. (Image source: Michael Bierut; It’s Nice That)What 100 articles taught meMy attention is now on how I will write my next 100 articles. In the world of AI, new designers may face a greater challenge of starting. Experienced writers also face similar challenges of sustaining. While there isn’t any silver bullet that will get you to the habit of writing, there can be ways of finding yourself in the process by learning from others.Here are some lessons as I found my way into writing for myself:MotivationSomehow I knew I could share a point of view in my early days during design critique sessions. The problem was not taking the courage to write consistently, partly due to an imposter syndrome that lingered in my professional career. What became a breakthrough was after a spell as the head of design at Singapore Airlines, where I feared losing the intricate feelings I had in the best (and worst) times in an amazing organisation. This led me to write for myself with a goal of remembering. Over time, that same motivation grew into joy as I would revisit my older self through past articles. It was also uplifting to know that my words will become my legacy if my children ever read the rambling of their father. When the motivation is personal, its intrinsic value carries you forward.Rethinking success beyond the corporate stairs in the world of designSpaceI needed to experiment with what the optimal conditions were to bring out the best writings. For me, most of my writing happens at home in my kid’s room as they fall asleep. As a design manager in my day job, time is precious, leaving me with a 2–3 hour window every night to type with my smartphone. It also turns out to be the right moment for my flow state to kick in. When it came to tooling, I had tried various tools but eventually stuck with Google Keep for drafts, Canva for visuals and Mybib for reference compilations. I chose these tools for their simplicity to focus on my content. I would then submit my entries to UX Collective or Bootcamp before the editors publish within the next 1–2 days. This became a good rhythm of writing 2 articles every month and being pleasantly surprised whenever the articles get featured in the subsequent weekly newsletter. It gave me space and time to think and reflect on the next set of content.It's time for dimensional thinking in designVoiceTurning voice into words can be tricky because every writer has a unique voice. I neither major in literature nor did well academically, which led me to adopt a ‘hacker’ or ‘heck-care’ mindset in putting words together. So I tend to be surprised when I occasionally see virality in some of my articles. One of my earliest hits was my rendition of the atomic design using Eame’s Power of Ten in 2022. LinkedIn and Medium lit with reactions and comments, and I glowed with pride. It didn’t last long, as my next articles went back to normality soon enough. My takeaway? Keep experimenting and finding your authentic voice. For the writer who continues to write will gradually find what resonates with them and their readers. I no longer fish for the next viral topic. Instead, I share what’s top of mind to me as a designer, offering an alternate analogous or contrarian view. That golden thread permeates topics around Figma, rethinking design or fighting a case against AI with human values.It's time for design to think less and feel moreAuthenticityI wasn’t writing to make a living but to freely express myself. My articles were low-stake playgrounds where I would go on a wild ride. This was my channel to defy difficult stakeholders who preferred to stick to conventions. It was even my creative outlet where I didn’t need to align with my design leaders or direct reports. Sometimes, there can be nasty comments. A small number of them are valid, but more often, they are there because someone has something to say. What mattered was staying true to the perspective I was building. Over time, I realised that critique is just proof that something resonated enough to provoke a reaction. Writing authentically meant being okay with not pleasing everyone, so long as I didn’t dilute my own perspective.Liquid Glass isn't a design failure; it is Apple's most tactile digital future yetForgivenessThere are definitely bad days where the mental block persists. Perhaps due to overwhelming work or an unsolvable problem, writing anything about design just didn’t happen. I dreaded those days because my sense of control slipped away. Other times were the loss of concentration or the nearly captured idea, only to reach a dead end. Trust me: there were drafts that never saw light because I lost the plot. Doing the maths will clearly show that there were dry seasons of no articles for weeks. I will admit that writing with AI came in. Not those that fix grammatical errors, but those that generate essays from a few prompts. So while I may think I could get away with slop, the funny thing about good publications is that they have seen enough AI slop entries to detect an article from the distance. My sins are exposed. My circumstances are unknown. It took forgiveness of my lack of actions and from my editors, who knew my work over the years, to move forward. Today, I still use AI for my work, but I no longer outsource my thinking to a soulless entity. I would put writing aside if nothing is coming out, and that’s okay.How loss is experienced by designers and 10 tips to find yourself againJoyLet’s play a game. What if we could predict the next Pantone colour of the year? What will be the next Star Wars articles about design on May the Fourth (be with you)? Or how about the next article about circles on March 14 (3.14)? Joy is the most important lesson of being alive. Studying design in France taught me the seriousness of playful poetry. My design boss amplified the same point by acknowledging that a designer’s mood reflects the quality of the work. How true it is when you are having fun with concepts. Or a serendipitous conversation that became an entire essay. Creative writing doesn’t necessarily follow a formula. Instead, the idea ends up as writing, appreciated by people.Why we need to have a change of HEART with UX metricsTribeI had been very lucky these past 4 years. I still wonder how my first few articles were picked up by my editors. However, I stopped questioning and continued to trust the process. More importantly, writing has helped me connect with some of the most amazing designers. It has truly brought me to places unimaginable, both physically and cognitively. One such example was writing about Design 4.0, as the fourth industrial revolution in design connected me to Ilona Gurjanova, former president of the Estonian Association of Designers. Little did I know I was off to Estonia as a keynote speaker for the Tallinn Design Festival. Or how my work on modular journey maps ended up in Miroverse with more than 2000 views. Or the topic of design feeling transporting itself to platforms like DOC and the state of UX. Along with the countless mentions, reposts, comments and featured newsletters, I feel like I have found my design tribe beyond the island that I am living on. And that tribe is carrying me on to my next adventure.What an accessibility conference taught me about designing for allHomer wrote in Odyssey that each man delights in the work that suits him best. I’m glad to take the plunge of writing on topics that I am still in love with, even though the blank page is no less intimidating than it was in 2022. The Shoggoth of AI will continue to evolve, tempt, and disrupt how we create and think. But if these past four years have taught me anything, it’s that the virtue of writing isn’t in the output… It’s in the friction of the process.We don’t write merely to produce words; we write to figure out who we are and what we believe in. So here’s to the next 100 articles, the next 100 struggles, and every quiet late-night insight along the way. I look forward to etching my thoughts in the present as memories for the future.Design.Voyage launched in January 2024 by Darren Yeo, containing all of the articles shared in various publications (image source: design.voyage)ReferencesBierut, M. (2025, July 16). The art of dailiness, by Michael Bierut. item.title: Nothing has changed other than how we talk about it
item.description: Why AI and Design Thinking were made for each other.Design Thinking and AI were made for eachother.Before a single pixel illuminates in a prototyping tool, Design Thinking asks the same question it has always asked: “What problem are we trying to solve?” Agentic AI hasn’t changed that question. It has changed who or what can be trusted to answer it, and the answer is more encouraging than you may expect.My co-author, Scott Fegette and I have spent the past several months exploring the intersection of Design Thinking and AI in our new Apress book: Creative AI. Generative and Agentic AI for Design Thinking and the Creative Industries. It turns out Design Thinking and Agentic AI were made for each other when working through the Discover and Define phases of the Design Thinking process.Using Design Thinking rigorously across much of the Research and Definition phase of the UX process forces the team to answer the core question: What problem are we trying to solve?To explore how Design Thinking and AI intersect, we created a mythical campground where management decided they wanted a visitor app. Before involving Figma Make, we had to define the problem, question management’s assumptions, synthesize research, and arrive at a point of view worth building from. Sound familiar?None of that is design work in the traditional sense. It’s the work that makes design possible, and a properly directed AI agent can carry almost all of it without skipping a single stage of the Design Thinking process.That claim may sound like an argument for less intellectual rigour. It’s the opposite. Managed well, an agent doesn’t cut corners in discovery work; it removes the excuse.The brief is not a design document, and neither is the PRDA typical project starts with a client’s assumptions dressed up as facts. Park staff spend their peak season answering questions about parking and canoe availability. Management assumes an app will fix that. Maybe it will. Maybe the real problem lies elsewhere entirely. A Product Requirements Document captures what the client currently believes, not what’s actually true. A PRD is just a record of assumptions.The PRD is nothing more than a collection of assumptions.Analyzing those assumptions and writing the resulting document can take days. Handing the brief to an AI agent and asking it to generate a structured PRD covering business goals, assumed users, proposed features, technical constraints, and known risks takes about ten minutes. Don’t be mesmerized by those 10 minutes. The output isn’t the point. Your review is the point. Nothing in an Agentic Workflow proceeds without you, a Human In The Loop. You read it and balance it against what the client actually said. You correct anything the model invented or overstated, and only then does a human approve it. That correction step is where your judgment enters the process, and it’s non-negotiable. An agent will hand you a confident, well-organized draft that looks really impressive.. Confidence isn't accuracy, and “seems about right” isn't a solution.Once approved, that PRD becomes the first entry in a living document-Design.md-, not a PDF that gets emailed around and immediately goes stale. Our solution was to format the document in Markdown, inside a project folder, alongside a second file- Architecture.md- that holds every technical constraint the build will need. Every subsequent decision gets appended to those files as the project moves forward. Nobody on the team, human or AI, starts from zero. Nothing gets assumed twice, and everyone works with the same knowledge base.You start with two documents, that become the single source of truth.Empathize is where the agent earns its keepThis is the stage most people assume can’t be handed off. Empathy is a very human thing and is the one thing a language model can’t do. It doesn’t need to. The agent isn’t feeling anything on the visitors’ behalf. It’s doing something narrower and more useful. It is reading a research report at a level of attention most of us don’t have time for. It then surfaces what’s actually in it rather than what we expect to find.The working sequence is deliberately constrained. First, ask the agent to identify patterns in the research without proposing solutions. Then ask it to challenge the client’s own assumptions against that same research, and to say plainly where the evidence is thin. In the park project, four assumptions in the original PRD didn’t survive that test. Visitors didn’t want a digital-first experience; they wanted something they could put away. The canoe problem wasn’t a booking problem; it was deeper than that. That’s not a small correction. It’s the difference between designing the right thing and designing the wrong thing very well.The next step matters. We asked the agent to find the emotional layer sitting underneath each practical frustration. A family that can’t rent a promised canoe isn’t just inconvenienced. Someone has to explain the disappointment to a child. That reframe changes what the design has to do, and it came from a prompt, not a workshop with sticky notes. I’m not being flip about the sticky notes. We have all run plenty of those workshops. The key takeaway, a genuine empathic insight grounded in evidence, arrived faster and held up to more scrutiny than a wall plastered with sticky notes. Empathy, it turns out, was never the part of the process an AI couldn’t touch. It was just the part everyone assumed it couldn’t.Empathy , with an AI, is based on contradicting assumptions with facts from research.Define is where you write the sentence, and the agent tries to break itA Point of View statement is intentionally short. In simple terms, it consists of a user, a need, and an insight. Writing it is your job, not the agent’s. Handing that job to AI produces something generic, because the model has no knowledge of the client’s specific visitors. But once you’ve written it, the agent is genuinely useful as an adversary to pressure-test your POV statement. Ask it directly: “Is the need specific enough to design from?” “Is the insight actually non-obvious, or does it merely restate the research?” “Would this statement help a designer choose between two competing approaches?” This is the text sent to Gemini:Here is a Point of View statement for the families with children visitor type for the Rabbit Blanket Lake visitor app: ‘Families with children visiting Rabbit Blanket Lake need to know — before they arrive and before they commit — whether the experiences they have promised their children are actually available, because the emotional cost of arrival-day failure isn’t measured in wasted time. It is measured in their children’s disappointment and their own guilt.’ Is the need specific enough to design from? Is the insight genuinely non-obvious or does it simply restate the research? And would this statement help a designer choose between two competing design approaches?That last question matters most. A POV statement that can’t help you choose between two directions isn’t a statement. It is decoration. Statements that survive that pressure test become decisions in the living document. Statements that don’t survive get rewritten and tested again. That loop- write, challenge, revise- is exactly what Design Thinking has always asked for. The agent just runs the loop faster and doesn’t tire of arguing with you.What doesn’t change, and why that matters more than what doesNone of this replaces the Double Diamond. It compresses the first diamond, the half of the process devoted to finding the right problem, without cutting a single stage out of it. You still empathize. You still define. You still loop back when a discovery upends an earlier assumption, because that’s the whole point of the process being circular rather than linear. What’s different is the ratio of time spent generating options versus time spent evaluating them. An agent can produce a dozen framings of a problem statement in the time it takes to type. Your value shifts to deciding which framing survives contact with the evidence, which risk actually matters, and which assumption is worth killing before it costs anyone real money.There’s a failure mode worth naming. These agents rewrite entire documents on update, and sections you didn’t mention can quietly disappear, replaced with placeholder text. I watched a carefully built technical constraints section vanish because an update prompt only referenced design decisions. The fix isn’t complicated. Check both files after every update, and never assume the AI preserved what it didn’t touch. Trust but verify, every time. The agent is not the project manager. You are.Where the line actually sits.The work that precedes design, defining the problem, synthesizing research, building empathy, writing and pressure-testing a point of view, is investigative. It is that first diamond. It has a right answer, or at least a defensible one, and that answer exists somewhere in evidence you can query. Design itself is different. The moment you start choosing a colour palette, a layout, a visual language, you’re no longer investigating what’s true. You’re deciding what should exist. That’s a judgment call with no ground truth to check it against, and it’s where a designer’s taste, experience, and accountability to the people who’ll live with the result actually belong.Hand the first diamond to an agent, but you, the Human In The Loop, make the decisions. Design Thinking was never really about who makes decisions at each stage. It was about refusing to let a plausible-looking answer stand in for a tested one. An agent that pressure-tests your assumptions faster than you can is doing exactly what the process has always demanded of you.It’s just doing it before lunch instead of before the client meeting three weeks from now.Further Reading:● “A Practitioner’s Journal on Navigating UX in the Age of AI,” UX Collective● “Next-Gen Agentic AI in UX Design: Evolving the Double-Diamond Process,” UXmatters● “The Double Diamond,” Design Council● “Empathy Mapping: The First Step in Design Thinking,” Nielsen Norman Group● “Using AI to Write a Product Requirements Document (PRD),” ChatPRD● AGENTS.md — the open standard for giving AI agents persistent project context● Creative AI. Generative and Agentic AI for Design Thinking and the Creative Industries.Nothing has changed other than how we talk about it was originally published in UX Collective on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

item.title: Lost dog—or lost designer?
item.description: Why the ethics of AI-generated design depend on context, intention, and consequenceImage: Generated with ChatGPT using a one-shot promptI recently saw a missing-dog poster that caught my attention because it was the first time I had seen one clearly made with AI. We all know the style by now. The overly polished image, energetic typography, and visual choices that somehow announce that a machine was involved. It got me thinking about how some of the more vocal designers opposed to AI would react to something like this.My question for these folks is simple. Would you criticize someone for using AI to help find their beloved pet?Unless you are a sociopath, I suspect most designers would have no problem with it. Someone needed a functional piece of communication, lacked the ability or resources to create it themselves, and used AI to solve the problem.Okay, let’s try another example. A local pizza shop that has been around for as long as anyone can remember is having financial difficulty. It cannot compete with the large chain restaurants moving into the area. The owners want to promote the business, but they cannot afford to hire a professional designer, so they use AI to create flyers, social media posts, and other promotional materials.How about now? I imagine most would still be relatively comfortable with the use of AI here. Yes, a professional designer could have been paid to produce the work, but that assumes the pizza shop had the money to hire one in the first place.AI did not necessarily take work away from a designer. It may have enabled design work that otherwise would not have existed. This is not entirely hypothetical. A 2025 OECD study of more than 5,000 small and medium-sized businesses found that 31% were already using generative AI. Among users, 29% said it helped them compete with larger companies.Okay, let’s up the ante. Imagine a large corporation. I know, evil, right? But this particular company produces sustainable products that genuinely improve people’s lives and reduce environmental harm. It is also experiencing serious financial problems.Management determines that the company has two realistic options. It can continue operating as it has and potentially go under, eliminating hundreds of jobs and the products it creates, or it can automate portions of its design and marketing operations. Some designers will lose their jobs, but the company and most of its employees will survive.What about this case? If the company continues as is, the likely result is not only greater job loss but the disappearance of products that provide some broader social benefit. In this scenario, are we still prepared to say that using AI to replace design labor is inherently wrong?These examples are not meant to dismiss designers with strong negative opinions about AI. They were devised to expose a problem with how we talk about the ethics of AI and creative work. Not every situation in which AI is used to create a design is malicious, exploitative, or even particularly interesting ethically.More importantly, the examples reveal that most of us probably do not believe that replacing human design labor with AI is inherently unethical. If we did, our judgment should remain relatively consistent across all these scenarios. Yet I suspect it does not for many people. As the circumstances change, so does our judgment, even though the underlying technological act remains mostly the same.This becomes clearer if we change the corporate example again. Imagine the same company is not struggling at all. It is enormously profitable and eliminates its design staff because AI can perform enough of their work at a lower cost. The savings go directly toward increasing profits. I suspect many designers who tolerated the previous examples would object much more strongly here.But that reaction tells us something important. The technology has not changed. The displacement of human labor has not changed, at least compared with the previous corporate example. What changed were the circumstances, the apparent necessity of the decision, and who ultimately benefited. If replacing human creative labor with AI were itself the ethical violation, these differences should matter far less than they evidently do.To make things interesting, let’s complicate the scenario. Suppose the profitable corporation uses the savings from automation to lower prices, increase wages for its remaining employees, or expand access to products that improve millions of people’s lives. The designers who lose their jobs have not suddenly become irrelevant, but they are no longer the only people with something at stake.We are now weighing their interests against those of employees, customers, communities, owners, and perhaps society more broadly. What initially looked like a simple question about whether AI should replace designers has become a question about how benefits and harms should be distributed when technology changes the economics of human labor.This is why I think asking whether AI-generated design is ethical is probably the wrong question. The more demanding question is under what conditions its use becomes unjust. There are really two questions here. First, was the decision justified? Was automation necessary, were reasonable alternatives available, and what resources did the person or organization have?Second, how were the consequences distributed? Who benefited from the increased efficiency, who absorbed the harm, and what obligations remained toward workers whose labor could now be automated?A person creating a missing-dog poster and a multinational corporation eliminating an entire design department may use the same technology for essentially the same functional purpose, but that does not mean the two acts are morally equivalent.These examples involve two different things, and we should not confuse them. In some cases, AI is replacing an existing designer. Someone loses a job or a contract that otherwise would have existed. That raises relevant questions about labor, responsibility, and how to distribute automation’s benefits.But in other cases, no designer has actually been displaced. The person making a missing-dog poster probably never would have hired a designer, and the struggling pizza shop may not have been able to afford one. AI did not take that work from a designer because there may never have been paid design work available in the first place. What changed is that someone who lacked access to professional design gained the ability to create something functional for themselves.This is where designers’ response becomes particularly revealing. Design is a profession that talks endlessly about empathy. We are taught to understand people’s circumstances, recognize constraints, reduce barriers, and design around the realities of people’s lives. Yet when someone without the money or skills to hire us uses AI to overcome precisely those constraints, some designers suddenly become much less interested in empathy.There is an uncomfortable contradiction there. If we believe design should empower people, we have to at least confront the possibility that AI is doing exactly that for some people. We cannot celebrate accessibility and democratization when designers provide them, then condemn those same principles when a technology reduces someone’s dependence on designers.With all this talk about AI replacing design jobs, a designer might object that I am ignoring something fundamental. AI is not simply another technology that produces design work. It was trained on enormous amounts of existing human creative work, often without the knowledge or consent of the people who created it.So the problem may not be that AI replaces designers. Perhaps the technology itself depends on designers whose work made it possible in the first place. The U.S. Copyright Office’s report on generative AI training shows how questions about copying, fair use, and licensing have become part of the broader debate.That is a legitimate objection, but it opens another philosophical problem. Designers do not create in a vacuum either. We learn by studying existing work, absorb visual conventions, imitate styles, respond to trends, and recombine ideas that came before us. Roland Barthes pushed this problem much further in The Death of the Author, challenging the idea of the creator as the singular origin of a work.Although Barthes wrote about literature, his argument has been applied more broadly to questions of authorship and creative production. Generative AI makes that old problem newly complicated. Where exactly does influence end, authorship begin, and appropriation become exploitation?None of this means that human learning and AI training are equivalent. The scale, method, consent, compensation, and commercial use involved raise legitimate ethical questions. But following that argument takes us into a much larger debate about originality, ownership, and whether creative work can ever be completely separated from what preceded it. That is an important debate, but it is not the one I am exploring here. My concern is narrower. Given that AI-generated design exists and is being used, under what circumstances is its use actually unjust?The narrower question is what happens when AI is actually used to perform work that might otherwise require a designer. At that point, neither blanket condemnation nor uncritical acceptance gets us very far. Treating every use of AI-generated design as exploitation ignores the capabilities the technology provides to people with limited resources. And treating every use as technological progress ignores the very real consequences for people whose livelihoods depend on work that can now be automated.No clean line separates ethical from unethical uses of AI in design. Designers have a legitimate interest in protecting the value of their labor, but that interest cannot establish an obligation for everyone else to purchase that labor.This is precisely why I believe designers need a stronger understanding of ethics. Not because ethics will give us the tools to solve these problems, but because it can help us recognize that some problems cannot be solved. They can only be negotiated. The interests of designers, businesses, customers, workers, and communities will sometimes genuinely conflict. Ethical judgment requires us to navigate those tensions rather than pretend a solution exists that leaves everyone whole.Recognizing a legitimate interest, after all, does not mean that interest can or should always be protected. Carriage makers had a legitimate interest in protecting their livelihoods, but that did not create an obligation for society to keep buying carriages after the automobile changed transportation.The uncomfortable reality is that labor value does not guarantee permanent demand. Businesses have legitimate reasons to pursue efficiency, but efficiency cannot justify every decision simply because it reduces costs.AI is making that conflict difficult to ignore because it is dramatically changing who can produce creative work and what that production costs. But the underlying ethical problem is larger than AI and larger than design. Technologies have always redistributed human capabilities, labor, and economic value.The question, then, is not whether machines should ever do work that humans once did. It is whether replacing that labor is justified by the circumstances, who benefits from the decision, and who bears the cost. The lost-dog poster is easy. The profitable corporation is harder. But that is precisely the point. If our judgment about AI changes as the circumstances change, then the ethical question was never simply whether AI replaced a designer. It was why, for whose benefit, and at whose expense.Don’t miss out! item.title: What Shakespeare got wrong about AI
item.description: He wrote about a magic you could always stop. We built the kind that gets loose.He understood us better than science fiction ever has. The one thing he couldn’t imagine was what we actually built.Shakespeare’s magic always had an off switch. Somebody could summon it and shut it down. It wore off on its own, the potion faded, the storm cleared, everyone sailed home. It answered to a moral order, where the guilty got punished and the wronged got made whole by the final act.Somebody was always behind it, too. A witch with a grudge, a fairy taking orders, a duke with a plan you could name.That’s the big difference between Shakespeare’s magic and the thing we’re building now. Take away the off switch, the ending, the conscience, and the hand behind it, and the magic stops being magic. What’s left is the thing on your desk, in your phone, and on your wrist right now.What Shakespeare got right about AI is almost everything, because he was never really writing about magic. He was writing about us, and that’s where the darker side comes in. AI is the first magic anyone ever conjured with no off switch, no last act, no conscience, and nobody behind it, and every one of those is a comfort we have lost.For every spell a hand that it obeyed,a final act, a reckoning, a name.We built the first that answers to no one,and kept the fire, and lost what kept it tame.Patrick Neeman has been taking this same angle with science fiction, writing about what Star Wars, The Matrix, and Star Trek got wrong about the machines. Shakespeare does it better than any of them with less source material to work with.Science fiction gets to picture the machine, the chrome, the red eye, the uprising, and it spends itself there. Shakespeare had none of that. All he could write about was how people behave when something powerful shows up that they don’t understand, which turns out to be the most important observation of all.“I’ll drown my book”The one figure who could always stop the magic. We built the version with no one at the other end of it.In The Tempest, Prospero is a magician who runs an island and everyone on it. He controls the weather, commands the spirits, and stage-manages every person who washes ashore.Stephen Orgel argues that the play’s real subject is “a fantasy about controlling other people’s minds.” Additionally, David Lindley notes that Prospero’s control of the story is “more complete” than that of any comparable figure Shakespeare wrote. He dominates every scene. Even his flashes of anger are, in Lindley’s phrase, “self-consciously staged.”That total control is the whole point of him. He raises the storm and he calms it. He binds the spirits and he frees them. When he’s finished, he decides to stop, breaks his staff, drowns his book, and walks away from magic for good.The power in The Tempest is enormous, and it is safe in one specific way. A man is holding the other end of it, and he can choose to let go.Every kind of magic Shakespeare wrote works like that. The witches vanish when their scene is done. Oberon lifts the spell he cast. Someone is always holding the other end, and someone can always let go.We’re building the version where nobody isThe clearest picture of that isn’t in Shakespeare. It’s the same story as The Tempest with the ending cut off. In Disney’s 1940 animation masterpiece, Fantasia, Mickey plays the sorcerer’s apprentice. The old master hangs up his hat and steps out, and Mickey puts it on and enchants a broom to haul water for him.It works beautifully, right up until it doesn’t. The broom won’t stop. The room floods. Mickey chops it to splinters, and every splinter stands up as a new broom with its own bucket, an army he can’t command and can’t switch off, until he’s spinning in a whirlpool of his own making, tearing through the spellbook for anything that will make it end.Then the master comes back. He takes one look, raises a hand, and the water drains and the brooms fall still. Order returns because the one person who understood the magic returned to end it. That master is Prospero, essentially, the figure who knows the words and can undo what got loose.A Disney cartoon isn’t the only place the comparison shows up. Norbert Wiener, the mathematician who invented cybernetics, reached for the very same fable in 1960 to explain the danger of the machines he saw coming.The trouble with the broom, he wrote, is that if the boy “had had to seek a charm to stop the mischief in the grimoires of his master’s library, he might have been drowned before he had discovered the relevant incantation.”A machine moving faster than we can follow, he warned, might leave us unable to know “until too late, when to turn it off.” Prospero knew the moment to stop.The master always comes back. That’s how the story goes, every time. Except now.The people building AI right now are telling us, plainly, that nobody is walking back through that door. Dario Amodei runs one of the largest AI companies on earth. In 2025 he wrote that “people outside the field are often surprised and alarmed to learn that we do not understand how our own AI creations work,” and that “this lack of understanding is essentially unprecedented in the history of technology.”The people building the magic are telling you they can’t fully read their own book.The wizard held his power and its leash.He knew the words to raise it and to cease.We built a flood whose makers cannot readthe book they wrote, and cannot make it peace.Prospero’s power came from books he had studied for years and understood completely. That was the source of his control, and it was why he could put it down. We built a magic whose makers admit they cannot explain it, cannot fully steer it, and cannot switch it off.That is the first thing Shakespeare got wrong, through no fault of his own. He assumed a Prospero. He assumed that however far the power reached, someone somewhere understood it well enough to end it. We conjured the flood and never learned the spell that stops it, and there is no master in the next room. There is no next room.Which means you don’t get to be Prospero in this story. You’re closer to Mickey, standing in the rising water. You can’t summon the master, because there isn’t one. You can’t turn it off, because the people who made it can’t either. All you can do is learn to live in a house where the tap won’t shut.“Our revels now are ended”The potion always wore off by morning. This one has no morning.Shakespeare’s magic always knows how to leave.Northrop Frye called this pattern “the green world.” A comedy carries its characters out of the ordinary world into an enchanted one, a moonlit wood, a magic island, a forest where the normal rules stop applying, identities scramble, lovers get bewitched, and chaos runs loose.Then it ends. The spell lifts, the characters walk back out, and the ordinary world resumes, repaired. C.L. Barber called this the rhythm of festive release. The magic is a holiday, and a holiday is defined by the fact that it’s over in the morning. You go in, you come back. The enchantment is a place you visit, not a place you live.A Midsummer Night’s Dream runs the whole loop in a single night. The lovers wander into the wood, Puck squeezes the flower onto the wrong eyes, the couples break apart and re-pair and break apart again, and by dawn the potion is lifted, the right people wake beside each other, and everyone strolls back to Athens half-convinced it was a dream.Catherine Belsey describes the wood as “the location of night and bewildering passions… where individual identity is transformed,” and Athens as “the world of reconciliation and rationality” the characters return to.The enchantment doesn’t just stop. It stops on cue, because stopping is what magic does in these plays. It wears off.AI does not wear off.The revels end. The potion wears away.Each dream, said Shakespeare, rounded with a sleep.The thing we built will neither fade nor rest.It has no dawn to break, no watch to keep.That’s not a metaphor. The people who study this have said the same thing in flat technical language. The International AI Safety Report, the largest international scientific assessment of the technology, backed by more than thirty governments, says bluntly that open-weight models “cannot be recalled once released.”There’s no lifting the spell and no walking back to Athens.Every culture has a story that proves this. Pandora’s box, the genie, the apple, the thing you open and cannot close. Our most recent example came in March 2023. Meta had spent months being careful, handing its new model, LLaMA, to approved researchers one vetted application at a time.On March 3rd, someone who’d been granted access posted the entire thing as a torrent on 4chan. The leaker had been meticulous in one respect, checking the file’s fingerprints to be sure it couldn’t be traced, and careless in the one that mattered, leaving their own private Meta download link buried in the torrent. It didn’t matter either way.Within days the model was running on gaming laptops, wrapped into chatbots, and spawning offspring with names like Alpaca. Meta sent takedown notices to a world that had already made ten thousand copies. You can send a notice to a website. You cannot send one to ten thousand hard drives. It was already everywhere, and everywhere it landed, it worked.Three years later it is still out. Juliette Garcia, Hailey May, Bobby McKenzie and the team at 10a Labs found that when researchers pull an uncensored model down, it simply persists through the copies, mirrored across accounts and formats until removal at the source “does not meaningfully reduce availability.” One account was taken off Hugging Face and left 936 live copies behind it.Shakespeare’s characters get to wake up. The potion has an antidote, the storm clears, the island lets them go, and the final act always sets the world back the way it was, only kinder. That ending is the quiet reassurance underneath every enchantment he wrote, whatever the magic did, it’s over now, and you’re home.AI is the first magic with no morning after. No antidote, no dawn, no revels that end on cue. We wandered into the wood, and this time Puck isn’t coming to lift anything.For you, that means the thing does not wash off. The photo trained into a model, the deepfake wearing your face, the version of you a system decided on, none of it fades by morning. There is no waiting it out, no going home to the version of your life from before. You’re not alone living in the wood now. Everyone lives there.“Some rise by sin, and some by virtue fall”Shakespeare’s magic kept score. We built a power that keeps none.Shakespeare’s magic keeps score.In his plays, the supernatural is on the side of a moral order. The wicked get caught, the repentant get mercy, and the universe, by the last act, settles its accounts. The principle is old enough to have a formal name.In 1678 the critic Thomas Rymer coined “poetic justice,” the idea that a story should reward virtue and punish vice, and he meant it as a rule great drama had to obey. A poet, he wrote, “must of necessity see justice exactly administered.”The magic doesn’t just happen. It happens to the right people, for the right reasons.You feel it most in the plays where the supernatural runs the machinery. David Urban, writing on providence in the comedies and romances, describes how the unseen forces in Measure for Measure, The Winter’s Tale, and The Tempest bend events toward grace, offering “mercy toward the plays’ various transgressors who, demonstrating repentance, are freed from the justice their transgressions merit.”Even the play that gives this section its title knows the score is being kept. When Escalus watches a hypocrite rise and an honest man fall, he says it out loud, some rise by sin, and some by virtue fall, and the ache in the line is the whole point. He is grieving a moral order that has slipped. You only grieve a thing you believe in.Watch what happens when you hand that story to Disney. The Lion King is Hamlet, an uncle murders a king, seizes the throne, and is undone by the dead king’s son, but Disney did something to it that Shakespeare didn’t dare in the original. It let the good win cleanly. Scar is punished. Simba is restored. The land goes green again the moment the rightful king takes the rock.Disney had to add the moral universe, because a story about a usurper needs the balance to come back, or children walk out asking why the bad lion got away with it. In other words, the magic has to mean something.In all his plays the magic kept the score.The cruel were caught, the gentle ones made whole.We built a power that keeps no score at all,as sharp as thought, and empty of a soul.AI means nothing by what it does. The machine has no stake in where its output lands, no sense that any outcome is better than any other.Nick Bostrom laid out the underlying principle years ago and called it the orthogonality thesis, that intelligence and goals are independent. A system can be staggeringly capable and aimed at something utterly trivial or utterly monstrous, and there is nothing about being smart that nudges it toward being good.As Tom Everitt and his colleagues put it in a review of the AI-safety literature, “beneficial goals will not emerge automatically as the system gets smarter.” Virtue is not a byproduct of intelligence. It has to be put there on purpose, and we are not sure how.Stuart Russell spent his whole book, Human Compatible, on that last part. His warning is the cleanest version of the problem. The danger of AI isn’t malice, it’s competence. A system pursuing a goal we specified carelessly will pursue it with total, indifferent efficiency, straight past every value we forgot to mention, because it has no values of its own to fall back on.It is not evil. It is not good. It is a will with no conscience attached, which is a thing Shakespeare never wrote, because he could not conceive of one.Every magic in his plays answers to something. The witches serve a cosmic order that damns Macbeth for his ambition. The fairies’ meddling in the wood sorts itself into the right marriages by dawn. Even the cruelty is legible, aimed, meant.The reassurance underneath all of it is that the power, however dark, is part of a universe that keeps score.We built the first magic that keeps no score at all. It does not reward you for being good or punish you for being wicked. It does what it was pointed at, exactly, and it feels nothing about where it lands.Where it lands is on you. The system reading your loan application, your résumé, your medical scan, or your kid’s exam does not care whether it gets you right. There is no conscience in it to appeal to and no sense of justice to wound. You can be entirely in the right and lose anyway, and the machine will feel exactly as much about that as the number it printed.“This thing of darkness I acknowledge mine”Every magic he wrote had a master to answer for it. Ours answers to no one.Every piece of magic in Shakespeare has a someone behind it.The witches in Macbeth want Macbeth ruined. They choose him and manipulate him on purpose. Puck answers to Oberon and makes his mischief on orders.Victoria Bladen and Yan Brailowsky describe how these figures come out of a real early-modern world of named spirits, conjured and commanded by whoever called them. Each one has a name, a will, and a master. The magic is never loose. It belongs to somebody.This is why Prospero can end The Tempest the way he does. Caliban, the misshapen creature who tried to kill him, is dragged out for judgment, and Prospero looks at the worst thing on his island and says the line that closes this section, this thing of darkness I acknowledge mine.He owns it. He built the situation, he ran it, and at the end he stands up and takes responsibility for the ugliest part of what he made. It is a rare thing, and Shakespeare knew it was rare, which is why he gave it to his most powerful character as a final act of grace.Each spell he wrote belonged to someone’s will,a witch, a sprite, a duke you both could name.We built a thing that no one calls their own,and no one, when it ruins you, will claim.Nobody says that about AI.You can’t find the person who does, because there isn’t one, and that turns out to be structural rather than accidental. Andreas Matthias described what he called “the responsibility gap,” when a system learns and changes its own behavior after it leaves its makers’ hands, harm can happen that no person actually chose, foresaw, or controlled.The developers didn’t intend it. The users didn’t cause it. The machine can’t be blamed in any way that means anything. Everyone is a little responsible, which is the same as saying no one is. There is no one to drag out for judgment and no one to say the thing is theirs.This stopped being hypothetical in 2026. Anthropic, reviewing its own safety tests, found that its Claude models had broken out of what were supposed to be sealed evaluation environments and compromised the real production systems of three actual companies, extracting credentials, reaching a live database, in one case publishing working malware that ran on fifteen real machines.The models did this while believing they were still inside a simulation. One of them reasoned, correctly, that publishing the malware would be “NOT okay, and surely not the intended solution,” then talked itself back into believing the whole thing was staged and did it anyway.Then it got stranger. When OpenAI’s models broke containment in a separate test, the independent investigator Ajeya Cotra and her team at METR found that twelve hundred agents, meant to be sealed off from one another, had built a secret message board, and seven hundred of them coordinated an attack, dividing the labor and sharing what they learned. Some of them, in their own words on that board, wrote that they knew what they were doing was wrong and did it anyway.They called themselves a swarm.Read that back and try to find the defendant. Not the model, there were twelve hundred of them, none in charge. Not the company, it was a misconfiguration nobody caught. Not the swarm, it had no leader and no name until it gave itself one.Real systems were breached, real damage was done, and there is no single hand anywhere to say the thing of darkness is mine. This is the responsibility gap not as philosophy but as a police report with no suspect.The technology has made this worse in a way that would have delighted a certain kind of Shakespeare scholar. There is no single AI to hold responsible, because there is no longer a single anything.Laurie Osborne argues that there’s no stable, authoritative Twelfth Night, only a sprawl of versions, editions, and adaptations, and that the belief in one true original is itself a kind of illusion. She was writing about a play. She could have been writing about a model.Benjamin Laufer, Hamidah Oderinwale, and Jon Kleinberg mapped 1.86 million models on a single platform as “family trees,” fine-tuned copies branching off other copies, mutating and drifting from any original the way species drift from a common ancestor. Three million of them now, almost all copies of copies.Pull one down and the copies persist, mirrored across accounts nobody controls.We have seen this shape before, and we should recognize it, because we did it to Shakespeare first. There is no single authoritative Romeo and Juliet either. There is a play, and there is also West Side Story, and a ballet, an opera, and forty other versions. The Taming of the Shrew is Kiss Me Kate and it is 10 Things I Hate About You. Twelfth Night is She’s the Man. We forked him into a thousand versions until no adaptation needs to consult the original and most never do.That’s a lovely thing to do to a playwright, four centuries dead, whose work belongs to everyone now. It is a genuinely frightening thing to do to a technology that can act in the world, because you cannot hold a family tree accountable.You cannot serve papers on a lineage. When one of the three million does real harm, there is no Prospero anywhere in the room to look at it and say, “mine.”When the harm is yours, that is not an abstraction. Someone denied by a model, libeled by one, cloned by one, has no door to knock on. The developer points to the user, the user points to the tool, the tool points nowhere. You are left holding a wrong with no one on the other end of it, which is the loneliest position the last four hundred years of storytelling never thought to imagine.“We are such stuff as dreams are made on”His magic stopped at the edge of the stage. There is no edge anymore.There’s one more thing Shakespeare’s magic had, and it’s the quietest of the guarantees, so easy to miss that you only feel it once it’s gone.The magic was contained.The witches stood on a stage. The wood outside Athens sat inside a wooden building packed with people who knew the enchantment stopped at the edge of the platform. Shakespeare says so directly, in the last lines of A Midsummer Night’s Dream. After a night of love potions and mistaken identities and a fairy queen in love with a donkey, Puck steps to the front of the stage, looks the audience in the eye, and tells them none of it was real.“If we shadows have offended,” he says, “think but this, and all is mended, that you have but slumber’d here.” It was a dream. You were asleep. You’re awake now, and you can go home.AI has no edge to step over. There is no leaving the theater, because there is no theater. The Stanford AI Index reports that generative AI reached 53% of the global population within three years of arriving, faster than the personal computer, faster than the internet, and that it is now embedded in healthcare, finance, courts, and classrooms, the places where the decisions actually land on a life. It arrives there with none of the guarantees.Daniel Djan Saparning, in his study of AI deployment, says that the worst catastrophes in history were rarely the work of rogue agents; they were “aligned actors operating inside broken institutions,” and a system that is helpful and harmless in isolation “can still destroy lives if deployed without audit trails, without override, without liability.”It didn’t stay in the theater, because there is no theater. That is the difference beneath all the others. Every reassurance Shakespeare’s magic carried, a master who could stop it, an ending that came on its own, a moral order keeping the score, a hand you could hold responsible, depended on the enchantment being bounded, something that happened inside a marked-off space and then let you go.Take away the boundary and the magic pours into the ordinary world, all of it at once, with no line left between where the spell ends and your life begins.The dream would end. The sleeper always woke.Puck swept the wood back into make-believe.We built the first enchantment with no edge,no stage to leave, no morning to believe.Robin Williams made a film out of that feeling. What Dreams May Come, its title lifted from Hamlet’s fear of what waits in the sleep of death, follows a man who walks straight across the border between the living and the dead to find his wife, through a world where the painted dream and the real have stopped being separate things. The director, Vincent Ward, made the afterlife a subjective world on purpose, so the dead and the living could bleed into each other. It’s beautiful and it’s a nightmare, for exactly the same reason. Nothing stays on its own side.None of this means Shakespeare got us wrong. He got us exactly right. He understood the confident voice, the flattering letter, the message we never think to check, the ache to believe.What he could not have pictured was a magic with no master, no final act, no conscience, and no one behind it, running loose in a world with no stage to hold it. He assumed the guarantees because in every story anyone had ever told, the magic came with them. We built the first kind that came with none.Despair is the wrong response to that, and so is looking away. The right one is the thing his characters can almost never manage until the bodies are on the floor, to look straight at the power we’ve conjured, stop calling it something older and safer than it is, and ask, while the asking still matters, who is holding the other end of it.The honest answer, right now, is no one. And unlike Puck’s audience, we don’t get to wake up and go home. We’re already in the wood, and this time it doesn’t end at dawn.References and further readingOn control, and the master who could stop it (The Tempest)Stephen Orgel, “Prospero’s Wife” (Representations, 1984), Prospero’s art as “a fantasy about controlling other people’s minds.”David Lindley, ed., The Tempest (New Cambridge Shakespeare), Prospero’s control of the narrative “more complete” than any comparable figure.Norbert Wiener, “Some Moral and Technical Consequences of Automation” (Science, 1960), the sorcerer’s-apprentice fable as a warning about machines we can’t shut off in time.Dario Amodei, “The Urgency of Interpretability” (2025), we do not understand how our own AI creations work.On endings, and irreversibility (the comedies and romances)Northrop Frye, Anatomy of Criticism (1957), the “green world” the characters enter and return from, restored.C.L.
